rich_summary: This section explains a divine chain of curses that sets up the birth of key figures in the Mahabharata. King Mahabhisha, a righteous ruler who reached heaven through great sacrifices, gazes improperly at the river‑goddess Ganga when her garments are blown aside in Brahma’s court. For this lapse he is cursed to be reborn on earth, and Ganga is destined to cause him suffering there. Meanwhile the celestial Vasus are cursed by the sage Vasishtha to be born as humans after they unknowingly offend him. They beg Ganga to become their mother on earth and release them quickly by casting them into the river after birth. She agrees, but asks that one child survive. That surviving son—destined to be childless—will later be the great Bhishma, tying the cosmic curses to the origins of the Kuru dynasty.

highlight_spans.why: Declares the Mahabharata’s sacred status, equating it with the Vedas and stressing the merit gained by hearing it.
The moment Mahabhisha gazes at Ganga when her garments are displaced—an impulsive act that triggers the curse driving the story.
Brahma’s curse on Mahabhisha, establishing his rebirth on earth and linking his fate with Ganga.
The Vasus explain their own curse from the sage Vasishtha, expanding the theme of divine law and consequences.
Ganga agrees to cast her newborn children into the river so the Vasus may quickly escape human life—an essential setup for Bhishma’s birth.
The striking scene where the beautiful Ganga sits on King Pratipa’s lap, initiating the fateful connection between the river goddess and the Kuru lineage.

top_scenes.scene_text: In Brahma’s celestial court, the wind lifts Ganga’s white garments while the gods avert their eyes but King Mahabhisha stares, drawing the anger of Brahma.
The radiant river-goddess Ganga meets the sorrowful Vasus on a heavenly path as they plead with her to be born as their mother on earth.
At the banks of the Ganga, the beautiful celestial maiden rises from the water and sits upon the meditating King Pratipa’s thigh as he performs austerities.
